env.setupHint: This may take a few minutes on first setup

presets.title: Scenario Preset
presets.small_objectsDesc: Few classes, small objects, fast video. Optimized ROI with freeze.
presets.industrialDesc: Fixed camera inspection, defect detection. High precision, minimal augmentation.
presets.trafficDesc: Vehicles & pedestrians, many objects, scale variation. Dense scenes.
presets.edge_mobileDesc: Raspberry Pi, phones, IoT. Minimal size, maximum speed.
presets.medicalDesc: Lesions, cells, high precision. Conservative LR, heavy freeze.
presets.aerialDesc: Drone/satellite imagery, tiny objects, any orientation. High resolution.

waiting.pro: First complete epoch hasn't finished yet. Once it does, we'll read train_loss, val_loss and the target metric to begin diagnosing.

warmingUp.pro: {{n}} of 3 minimum epochs. With so few points any trend is noise: at least 3 samples are needed to estimate loss and metric slopes. Holding off on judgment.
warmingUp.fun: Warming up 🏃 ({{n}}/3), too early to judge

healthy.pro: Healthy training: train_loss is decreasing and the target metric improves ≈{{rate}}%/epoch over the recent window. This is the expected scenario; if it holds until the schedule ends, nothing to tweak.

excellent.pro: {{metric}} = {{value}}% — very high. Before celebrating, validate on an independent test set to rule out overfitting or train/val data leakage. If confirmed, this checkpoint is ready to export.
excellent.fun: Crushing it, {{metric}} {{value}}%! Validate on test too ⚡

strong.pro: {{metric}} = {{value}}% is a competitive level. There's usually additional margin by dropping the learning rate (lr0 × 0.1) in final epochs, or extending training with strong augmentation for better generalization.
strong.fun: Looking sharp ({{metric}} {{value}}%). A bit of polish ✨

overfitting.pro: Overfitting signal: train_loss still drops but val_loss has started to rise. Means the model is memorizing train instead of generalizing. Still mild — if it persists 5-6 more epochs, raise weight_decay, strengthen augmentation (mosaic, mixup, hsv), or enable early stop.
overfitting.fun: Starting to memorize 📚. If it keeps up, more aug.

overfitSevere.pro: Sustained severe overfitting: the val_loss − train_loss gap grew to {{gap}} and keeps widening over several epochs. The model no longer generalizes. Restore the best previous checkpoint and relaunch with more regularization (weight_decay, dropout, augmentation) or more data.
overfitSevere.fun: Serious overfit 🚨 gap {{gap}} and growing. Back to best.

valLossUp.pro: val_loss rising without matching progress in train_loss. Different from classic overfitting: here the model isn't learning train well either. Typical suspects: LR too high for this stage, noisy data, or batch-norm conflicting with a small batch.
valLossUp.fun: Val angry for no reason 😤 check LR and data.

lrTooHigh.pro: train_loss oscillates with coefficient of variation {{cv}}% and multiple sign changes, failing to descend. That's the classic too-high LR pattern: steps overshoot the minimum. Try halving lr0 or enabling cos_lr for smooth decay.
lrTooHigh.fun: Loss bouncing (CV {{cv}}%). LR too high, drop it.

lrTooLow.pro: After several epochs, the metric barely moves and loss decreases very slowly. Probable cause: lr0 too small, or model underpowered for the task. Raise lr0 2-3×, try a larger model, or check pretrained=True.

boxDominates.pro: box_loss averages {{ratio}}× cls_loss in the recent window. Training is focusing hard on locating boxes and little on classifying. If classification matters as much as detection, raise the 'cls' weight in loss config.
boxDominates.fun: box eats cls ({{ratio}}×). Bump cls weight.

clsDominates.pro: cls_loss averages {{ratio}}× box_loss. The model classifies well but localizes poorly, or there's strong class imbalance. Check class distribution and consider raising the 'box' weight.

dflHigh.pro: dfl_loss high vs box_loss means the box-coordinate distribution isn't converging: imprecise boxes. Raise the 'dfl' weight or improve annotation quality/consistency.

regression.pro: {{metric}} dropped from {{best}} to {{now}} over {{epochs}} consecutive epochs. This is no longer punctual noise: the model has steadily gotten worse. Worth comparing against the best checkpoint and, if the schedule has no recovery mechanism, stopping and reverting to best.
regression.fun: Backing up for a while: {{metric}} {{best}}→{{now}} in {{epochs}} epochs 📉

earlyStop.pro: Best value hasn't been beaten in {{epochs}} epochs. No guarantee it won't improve later (LR schedules can revive the model), but statistically the ROI is decaying — reasonable to stop and keep the best if compute time matters.
earlyStop.fun: {{epochs}} epochs with no new best. Stopping is fair 🛑

plateau.pro: Target metric barely moving in recent epochs. Could be a real stall or a plateau before another jump when LR decays. If cos_lr isn't active, manually dropping lr0 by ×0.1 often breaks plateaus.

plateauLow.pro: Stuck at {{value}}%, a low level to settle on. Typical causes: dataset too small or imbalanced, noisy labels, or model inadequate for the problem's complexity. Inspect the data before tuning hyperparameters.

converged.pro: Converged: {{metric}} = {{value}}% stable for several epochs. The model has squeezed what it could from this schedule. Extra epochs won't help; export and validate.

lossExploding.pro: train_loss spiked ×{{ratio}} ({{from}} → {{to}}). That's divergence: the optimizer went off the rails. Common causes: lr0 too high, AMP with bad scaling, or gradients without clipping. Lowering lr0 or disabling AMP usually fixes it.

nan.pro: NaN/Inf appeared in the loss. No recovery from that: weights are corrupted. Common causes: lr0 too high, AMP instability, corrupt images, or invalid annotations (boxes out of range, etc.). Must restart.

deadModel.pro: With {{metric}} = {{value}}% after {{epochs}} epochs, the model isn't learning. It's not a tuning issue — check the basics: properly formatted labels, pretrained=True, reasonable LR, and that the dataset actually contains what you want to detect.

precisionHigh.pro: Precision {{precision}}% with recall {{recall}}%: the model is conservative, only predicting when very confident and missing many positives. Useful if avoiding false positives is the priority; otherwise, lower the confidence threshold or raise the cls weight.

recallHigh.pro: Recall {{recall}}% with precision {{precision}}%: the model over-predicts with many false positives. Useful if missing positives is unacceptable; otherwise, raise the confidence threshold or tune NMS IoU.

valTooEasy.pro: train_loss ({{train}}) consistently above val_loss ({{val}}) is unusual. Usually indicates data leakage (same images in train and val) or a validation split easier than the training split. Inspect how the split was built.

noisy.pro: train_loss is decreasing but with high noise (CV={{cv}}%). Happens with small batches or very heterogeneous data: each batch gives a different signal. Increasing batch size, enabling AMP, or raising nbs stabilizes training.

warmupPhase.pro: Warmup phase active: LR is still rising from a low value toward lr0. Metrics in this stretch don't yet reflect real training behavior — wait for LR to stabilize.

lrDecayed.pro: Current LR is tiny compared to the peak: the scheduler has used up its decay range. At this stage the model barely changes. If there's no recent improvement, it won't come without resuming with a new cycle.
lrDecayed.fun: LR near zero. No juice to improve.

neutral.pro: No conclusive patterns in the recent window: no strong overfitting, no divergence, no convergence either. Keep training and observe.

result.description: Your model has been trained successfully.

params.lr_encoderDesc: Learning rate for the encoder backbone
params.grad_accum_stepsDesc: Number of steps to accumulate gradients
params.early_stoppingDesc: Stop training when validation loss plateaus
params.gradient_checkpointingDesc: Trade compute for memory — enables larger models
params.warmup_itersDesc: Number of warmup iterations before full LR
params.batchSizeDesc: -1 for auto (60% GPU memory). Larger = more stable gradients.
params.epochsDesc: Total passes over dataset. More = better convergence but slower.
params.imgszDesc: Input resolution. Quadratic impact on speed. Match to object size.
params.patienceDesc: Epochs without improvement before early stopping.
params.max_detDesc: Maximum detections per image. Lower = faster post-processing.
params.multi_scaleDesc: Random size variation per batch. Improves scale robustness.
params.rectDesc: Minimal padding respecting aspect ratio. More efficient for non-square images.
params.cacheDesc: Cache images in RAM (fast) or disk. Speeds up training significantly.
params.optimizerDesc: Auto selects the best optimizer for your YOLO version.
params.lr0Desc: Initial learning rate. Higher = faster but can be unstable.
params.lrfDesc: Final LR as fraction of initial: lr_final = lr0 × lrf.
params.cos_lrDesc: Cosine scheduler: smooth decay, better fine convergence than linear.
params.warmup_epochsDesc: Epochs where LR gradually ramps up from near-zero to lr0.
params.momentumDesc: SGD momentum or Adam beta1. Higher = smoother training.
params.weight_decayDesc: L2 regularization. Higher = stronger regularization against overfitting.
params.boxDesc: Localization loss weight. Increase for precise bounding boxes.
params.clsDesc: Classification loss weight. Increase with few classes.
params.dflDesc: Distribution Focal Loss. Set to 0 for YOLO26.
params.pretrainedDesc: Use COCO pretrained weights. Always recommended unless dataset is very large.
params.freezeDesc: Freeze first N layers (backbone). 0 = train all. Higher with small datasets.
params.ampDesc: FP16/FP32 mixed precision. Faster and less memory. Disable only if NaN errors.
params.nbsDesc: Nominal batch size for loss normalization. Rarely needs adjustment.
params.single_clsDesc: Treat all classes as one. For binary detection (object/no object).
params.warmup_bias_lrDesc: Learning rate for bias parameters during warmup.
params.valSplitDesc: Fraction of images for validation. 0.2 = 80% train, 20% val.
params.workersDesc: Data loading threads. More = faster loading but more CPU/RAM.
params.deviceDesc: Compute device. Auto detects the best available.
params.mosaicDesc: Combines 4 images. Great for dense scenes. Reduce with small objects.
params.close_mosaicDesc: Disable mosaic for last N epochs. Stabilizes final training phase.
params.mixupDesc: Blends two images with transparency. Light regularization.
params.translateDesc: Random horizontal/vertical shift as fraction of image size.
params.scaleDesc: Random zoom variation. Increase if objects vary in apparent size.
params.fliplrDesc: Horizontal flip probability. Disable if laterality matters.
params.flipudDesc: Vertical flip probability. Enable for aerial/microscopy images.
params.degreesDesc: Random rotation range in degrees. 180 for aerial (any orientation).
params.shearDesc: Shear deformation in degrees. Use sparingly.
params.hsv_hDesc: Color hue variation. Keep low if colors are diagnostically relevant.
params.hsv_sDesc: Saturation variation. Reduce for controlled lighting.
params.hsv_vDesc: Brightness variation. Increase for variable lighting conditions.
params.erasingDesc: Random erasing simulates occlusion. Reduce with small objects.
params.freeze_encoderDesc: Freeze encoder weights for transfer learning
params.do_reduce_labelsDesc: Shift label IDs by 1 (some datasets use 255 for background)
params.warmup_ratioDesc: Fraction of training for linear warmup
params.angle_versionDesc: Angle encoding for oriented bounding boxes
params.window_sizeDesc: Window size for time series processing
params.max_prediction_lengthDesc: Maximum number of time steps to predict
params.max_encoder_lengthDesc: Maximum number of time steps for encoder input
params.gradient_clip_valDesc: Gradient clipping value to prevent exploding gradients
params.hidden_sizeDesc: Hidden layer size for the model
params.contaminationDesc: Expected fraction of anomalies in the dataset
params.n_estimatorsDesc: Number of estimators for ensemble methods
params.max_iterDesc: Maximum number of iterations for clustering
params.d_modelDesc: Dimension of the model's hidden representation
params.testSplitDesc: Fraction of images for hold-out test set. 0 disables test split.

labels.title: How to choose
labels.referenceCaveat: Published metric on a different dataset. Useful to compare families with each other, not to predict what your corpus will give.
labels.vramCaveat: Estimate with the backend's default settings.
labels.minSamplesCaveat: An order of magnitude, not a limit: below it a simpler family usually does better.
labels.licenseVaries: Each model in the repository carries its own: check its card.
labels.licenseInherited: The base model's license is inherited by the model you train and travels with it to deployment.
labels.noBiomedicalYet: There are no biomedically pretrained models in the catalog yet. Families marked biomedical are generalist architectures that work well on this imaging with the right preset.

radiography.use: Chest X-ray, especially with few labels: pretrained on 882,775 real films, which is exactly where an ImageNet backbone falls short.
radiography.avoid: Other modalities, and any direct clinical use: the authors state it is not meant for clinical practice.

beit.use: Strong self-supervised pretraining, useful when you have many images and few labels.
beit.avoid: With a modest GPU: the slowest in this backend.

convnext.use: A recommendable middle ground: transformer accuracy with CNN data requirements.
convnext.avoid: When the corpus is minimal: ResNet is better.

deit.use: Distilled ViT: same scheme, less data required.
deit.avoid: If you already have plenty of data: ViT or Swin reach higher.

swin.use: Good accuracy ceiling and robust to scale changes.
swin.avoid: With a small corpus or little VRAM.

vit.use: Transformer classification with ImageNet-21k weights; the path towards biomedical backbones later.
vit.avoid: With a few hundred images, where a pretrained CNN does better.

conditional-detr.use: Faster convergence than plain DETR while keeping the same scheme.
conditional-detr.avoid: With a very small corpus, where any DETR falls short.

deformable-detr.use: When you want DETR without its slow convergence; also better on small objects.
deformable-detr.avoid: If YOLO already solves the problem: it still costs considerably more to train.

detr.use: The conceptual reference for transformer detection, useful as a baseline comparable with the literature.
detr.avoid: In real projects with little data: it needs the most images and epochs to converge.

mask2former.use: Top quality on overlapping instances, with a large GPU.
mask2former.avoid: With little VRAM: it trains at batch 1 and is still tight.

maskformer.use: Mask-based instances when objects overlap and a box is not enough.
maskformer.avoid: If one polygon per object is enough: YOLO-seg trains far faster.

convnext.use: More accuracy than ResNet while keeping the top-down scheme.
convnext.avoid: If the project is small or the machine modest: ResNet costs less for little difference.

hrnet.use: The architecture designed for pose: it keeps high resolution throughout and is the keypoint reference.
hrnet.avoid: If you need maximum CPU speed.

resnet.use: Default pose backbone: fast, stable and enough for most skeletons.
resnet.avoid: When you need very precise joints on small bodies within the image.

beit.use: When the accuracy ceiling rules and hardware is not a constraint.
beit.avoid: Almost any time you lack a large GPU: it is the heaviest in this backend.

dpt.use: Globally coherent masks in wide scenes.
dpt.avoid: When fine edges or speed matter.

mask2former.use: The most accurate option in this backend when a GPU is available: a clear step up from MaskFormer.
mask2former.avoid: With under 8 GB of VRAM or only a few hundred images.

maskformer.use: When you want semantic and instance segmentation under a single mask formalism.
maskformer.avoid: If you only need plain semantics: SegFormer does the same for less.

mobilevit.use: Segmenting on CPU or modest hardware without dropping to useless results.
mobilevit.avoid: If you want the best accuracy: it is a trade towards size.

segformer.use: Modern semantic segmentation with a good cost/accuracy balance and ready ADE20K weights.
segformer.avoid: With a small corpus: transformers need more data than a U-Net.

upernet.use: Many-class scenes that benefit from a decoder unifying scales.
upernet.avoid: Few-class projects, where the cost does not pay off.

autoencoder.use: Structured anomalies, when there is enough normal data to learn what normal is.
autoencoder.avoid: With little data: statistical methods do better for less.

ensemble.use: A robust default: it combines criteria and holds up well on dirty data.
ensemble.avoid: If you need to explain exactly why something was flagged.

proximity.use: Anomalies defined by neighbourhood: useful when being far from everything else is what is odd.
proximity.avoid: With lots of data: cost grows fast with size.

statistical.use: Anomaly detection with no heavy training: fast, explainable and a good first pass.
statistical.avoid: When the anomaly is a complex pattern rather than an extreme value.

gan.use: Imputation that preserves the signal's distribution, not just its mean.
gan.avoid: If you want stability: the hardest to train in this backend.

rnn.use: Sequential imputation when gaps are short and local order rules.
rnn.avoid: On long gaps: the transformer makes better use of distant context.

transformer.use: Imputing gaps using the context of the whole series and the other variables.
transformer.avoid: With very small gaps: plain interpolation is enough and needs no training.

deepar.use: When you want prediction intervals and not just a point value.
deepar.avoid: If you only need the central point: N-HiTS costs less.

nbeats.use: Powerful univariate forecasting with no feature engineering.
nbeats.avoid: If you have external covariates that matter: it does not use them.

nhits.use: A more efficient N-BEATS, better on long horizons.
nhits.avoid: When you need N-BEATS' interpretable decomposition.

tft.use: Forecasting with several covariates when you also need to know what drove the result.
tft.avoid: Simple, short series: the most expensive in this backend for little gain.

rfdetr.use: Good modern accuracy/speed balance, with an Apache-2.0 license fit for closed products.
rfdetr.avoid: If you need arbitrary resolutions: it requires multiples of 32 and nothing below 320 px.

rtdetr.use: When you want transformer accuracy without YOLO's NMS and have GPU to spare.
rtdetr.avoid: With few images or a small GPU: it converges slower than YOLO and needs more memory.

rtdetrv2.use: Refined RT-DETR with more sizes to pick from; the S variant fits where RT-DETR-L does not.
rtdetrv2.avoid: If the corpus is small: it is still a DETR and needs more data than YOLO.

boosting.use: First choice on tabular data: XGBoost and LightGBM are what wins in practice.
boosting.avoid: With very few rows, or when you need a trivially interpretable model.

ensemble.use: Random Forest as a solid baseline that needs almost no tuning.
ensemble.avoid: When chasing peak performance: boosting usually wins.

linear.use: When interpretability rules or there are very few rows.

neighbors.use: A baseline with no assumptions about the shape of the data.
neighbors.avoid: With many columns: distance loses meaning and performance drops.

neural.use: When there are plenty of rows and the interactions are complex.
neural.avoid: On tabular data with little data: boosting almost always wins and needs less tuning.

svm.use: Few rows with many columns and a non-linear boundary.
svm.avoid: With thousands of rows: it scales poorly against boosting.

deeplab.use: When you need a wide receptive field without losing resolution: its dilated convolutions are the CNN reference.
deeplab.avoid: With a limited GPU or few images: much heavier than U-Net for little gain.

dpt.use: Dense prediction with a transformer when global mask coherence matters more than the edge.
dpt.avoid: If you want speed or have little data: one of the slowest in the family.

fpn.use: Objects at varied scales at a lower cost than PSPNet or DeepLab.
fpn.avoid: With uniformly scaled objects, where the pyramid adds nothing.

linknet.use: The lightest of the family: good for real time or a small GPU.
linknet.avoid: When object boundaries must be crisp: it trades detail for speed.

manet.use: When objects come in very different sizes within the same image: that is what its multi-scale attention is for.
manet.avoid: If U-Net already gives you the result: it adds cost with no guaranteed gain.

pan.use: Balance of speed and accuracy when LinkNet falls short and U-Net does not improve.
pan.avoid: If you already have a working U-Net: the change is rarely noticeable.

pspnet.use: Scenes with heavy context where what surrounds the object matters, not just the object.
pspnet.avoid: With small masks or fine detail: its region pooling blurs edges.

segformer.use: Efficient transformer: generalizes better than CNNs at a contained cost.
segformer.avoid: Below a few hundred images, where a U-Net with a pretrained encoder wins.

unet.use: Default starting point for segmentation, and the de facto standard in biomedical imaging. Works with few masks.
unet.avoid: In complex scenes with many context classes, where pyramid architectures capture the global picture better.

upernet.use: Complex multi-class scenes that need context unified across scales.
upernet.avoid: One- or two-class projects: too much architecture for the problem.

matrix-profile.use: Finding motifs and discords with no training and no labels: an ideal exploratory pass.
matrix-profile.avoid: When you need a classifier: it describes the signal, it does not predict labels.

radimagenet.use: Little labelled data on CT, MRI or ultrasound: starts from a backbone trained on 1.35 million radiology images instead of ImageNet photos.
radimagenet.avoid: Outside radiology. On histology or clinical photography its pretraining adds nothing, and a generic ConvNeXt does as well or better.

pathology.use: Already-extracted histopathology tiles: pretraining on H&E captures tissue texture an ImageNet backbone does not see.
pathology.avoid: Commercial use: both weights are non-commercial and that condition is inherited by the model you train. It also does not read whole slides — this takes tiles, not WSI.

convnext.use: A modern CNN that matches transformers while needing less data than they do. A good middle ground.
convnext.avoid: If the corpus is genuinely small: ResNet or EfficientNet remain safer.

efficientnet.use: Better accuracy than ResNet at similar cost; a good general choice with moderate data.
efficientnet.avoid: If you need maximum CPU inference speed: MobileNet is more direct.

eva.use: When you want the catalog's accuracy ceiling and have a large GPU.
eva.avoid: Almost always on a laptop: it goes past 16 GB of VRAM and is the slowest.

mobilenet.use: Classifying on CPU, mobile or browser with models of a few MB.
mobilenet.avoid: When accuracy matters more than size.

resnet.use: A mandatory baseline in classification: trains with few images, on CPU if needed, and is the control to measure everything else against.
resnet.avoid: When you are after the last point of accuracy and have the data and GPU for a transformer.

swin.use: Hierarchical transformer: a good accuracy ceiling and better than ViT with mixed object scales.
swin.avoid: With a small corpus or a limited GPU.

vit.use: With a medium or large dataset and a GPU: generalizes better than CNNs and is the basis of the biomedical backbones.
vit.avoid: With a few hundred images: without strong pretraining it lands below a ResNet.

cnn.use: Plain convolution: fast, interpretable and a good baseline.
cnn.avoid: With patterns at widely varying scales, where Inception covers more ranges.

inception.use: A strong baseline for series classification with a trainable architecture.
inception.avoid: With very few samples, where ROCKET wins at a fraction of the cost.

resnet.use: 1D ResNet: solid and fast for classifying signals.
resnet.avoid: When very long context is needed: a transformer captures it better.

rnn.use: Sequences where order rules and length is moderate.
rnn.avoid: On long series: slow to train and it struggles with distant dependencies.

rocket.use: First choice for series with very few samples: trains in seconds and is hard to beat.
rocket.avoid: If you need to tune the architecture or interpret the model: it is not trained by gradient.

tcn.use: A convolutional alternative to RNNs: trains faster and captures long context with dilations.
tcn.avoid: If the signal is short: a plain CNN is enough.

transformer.use: Long series with distant dependencies, when there is enough data.
transformer.avoid: With a few hundred windows: it overfits before it learns.

xception.use: Separable convolution: more capacity than the plain CNN at similar cost.
xception.avoid: If Inception already works for you: the difference is usually marginal.

kmeans.use: Grouping series by shape while allowing time shifts, using DTW.
kmeans.avoid: With many long series: DTW is expensive.

kshape.use: Grouping by normalized shape, invariant to amplitude and offset.
kshape.avoid: If the time shift is what you want to capture: DTW handles it better.

yolo.use: First choice for detection: trains fast, tolerates small datasets and exports to almost any runtime.
yolo.avoid: When you need maximum accuracy regardless of speed, or when the AGPL-3.0 license does not work for shipping your product.

filters.noneMatch: No model in this backend matches the filters.
